title: Famous brand mascots and the design lessons behind 12 icons
summary: Brand mascots are back. Explore 12 famous brand mascots, the design decision behind each and how to build a character that stays on-brand as it scales.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


Brand mascots are back, and the evidence says they work: campaigns built on recurring characters are 37% more likely to grow market share and 30% more likely to grow profit. The 12 icons here each win on one confident design decision their brands have held for years or even decades. What keeps a character alive is the system around it (a character bible, format specs and motion rules), which is also what lets a mascot scale across social, ads and video without drifting.


For two decades, most of us saw brand mascots as relics, cheerful hangovers from the print era and Saturday-morning cartoons. That view has changed, with research showing that campaigns built on characters and other recurring devices are[37% more likely to grow market share](https://lbbonline.com/news/research-by-system1-shows-memorable-characters-in-ads-boost-chances-of-profit-by-30) .


The 2025 Super Bowl proved that many leading brands take them seriously.[The game featured a full mascot resurgence](https://digiday.com/marketing/mascot-embrace-celeb-overload-and-metatextual-advertising-trends-dominating-this-years-super-bowl-ads/) in TV commercials, including an Instacart spot that assembled the Jolly Green Giant, the Pillsbury Doughboy, Chester Cheetah and the Energizer Bunny. At an event where big money usually goes to celebrities, brands used these playful characters to stand out.


The revival[goes well beyond the Super Bowl](https://strategyonline.ca/2026/03/16/2026-spring-strategy-magazine-upfront-mascots/) . Hotels.com's Bellboy, Mucinex's returning Mr. Mucus and McCain's Spud are all part of the 2026 wave, while Duo, Scrub Daddy, Pop-Tarts and Mr. Peanut have helped usher in what Adweek calls the["unhinged mascot era."](https://www.adweek.com/brand-marketing/brands-unhinged-mascot-social-media-mcdonalds-scrub-daddy-duolingo/)


Philippe Garneau of GWP Brand Engineering summed up why the timing makes sense when he spoke to Strategy magazine:


Mascots are antidotes to digital fatigue in an era when screens bombard us with identical AI-generated visuals lacking narrative depth.


Philippe Garneau


President and CCO, GWP Brand Engineering


**A distinctive character can give your brand a recognizable face, personality and point of view.** But can your brand create a mascot with enough character, consistency and flexibility to last?


Below, we break down 12 famous brand mascots, why they succeeded and the systems that turned them into enduring brand assets.


## 12 famous brand mascots and the design lesson behind them


The brands behind every example below made one confident decision and stuck with it. We explore the design choices that gave each character its distinct identity and share a lesson from each to guide your own work.


### 1. Bibendum the Michelin Man (Michelin)


Bibendum is one of the oldest mascots still in active service.[The idea started in 1894](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelin_Man) , when the Michelin brothers spotted a stack of tires at the Lyon Exhibition that looked like a man, and the character appeared in his famous poster four years later, in 1898. **He's one of the clearest examples of good design logic on this list.** Bibendum is built from stacked tires, so the character communicates the product before you read a word.


The mascot has also aged remarkably well, slimming and simplifying across more than a century while staying instantly identifiable. He's proof that a strong underlying concept can survive any number of redraws.


**Design lesson:** The best mascot is often the product wearing a face.


### 2. Mr. Peanut (Planters)


(Source:[Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division](https://picryl.com/media/mr-peanut-sign-hair-affair-sign-route-6-swansea-massachusetts-9498e1) )


A monocle, a top hat and a cane turned a peanut into a gentleman, a concept Planters has kept since 1916. The product itself was ordinary. **Mr. Peanut gave it personality, status and a character competing peanut brands lacked.**


In 2020, Planters staged the character's death and rebirth in a Super Bowl campaign, a stunt that worked because audiences were attached enough to react. You can't kill off a logo. You can kill off a mascot, which shows how much more emotional equity a character can carry.


**Design lesson:** A well-crafted mascot can give a commodity a personality the product can't create on its own.


### 3. Tony the Tiger (Kellogg's)


(Source:[Wikimedia Commons, Life Magazine](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Garry_Moore_Tony_the_Tiger_1955.jpg) )


Tony the Tiger has been redrawn many times since he debuted on Kellogg's cereal boxes in 1952. Over time, the character grew more upright, athletic and confident. Side by side, the change looks dramatic.


In sequence, nobody really noticed.


**This kind of controlled evolution is critical to building an enduring mascot.** Tony's silhouette, colors and personality stayed recognizable while his rendering was gradually updated, which is exactly how a character survives a[brand redesign](https://www.superside.com/blog/brand-redesign) without losing the recognition it spent decades building.


**Design lesson:** Make your character work for a new era, but don't change its key recognition triggers.


### 4. Colonel Sanders (KFC)


The Colonel is an unusual mascot because he was a real person.


KFC turned founder Harland Sanders into a simplified graphic icon, which places him somewhere between a portrait, a mascot and a logo. That's why he appears in our roundup of[30 famous logo designs](https://www.superside.com/blog/30-famous-logo-designs) as well as in lists of recognizable mascots.


The fast-food giant has also proved how flexible the character in the white suit and bow tie can be.


**KFC cast actors such as Rob Lowe and Reba McEntire as the Colonel, while the illustrated face stayed a constant part of the brand identity.**


**Design lesson:** A character can be both a brand identity system and a logo if the drawn version is strong enough to stay the brand's anchor.


### 5. The GEICO Gecko (GEICO)


The GEICO Gecko, one of the most famous animal mascots, is almost absurdly basic: a simply drawn reptile with a warm accent.


GEICO introduced him in 1999, and he went on to become one of the most recognizable mascots in American advertising.


**The gecko proves that a mascot doesn't need visual complexity to be memorable.** His simple design, distinctive voice and likable personality made him easy to recognize and easy to reproduce.


**Design lesson:** Simplicity can be a smart production choice. A straightforward design is practical to use at scale.


### 6. M&M's spokescandies (Mars)


M&M's animated characters each have a face, arms and legs, with a distinct personality tied to their color. Red is cynical, Yellow is happy and gullible and Blue is the cool one. **The comedy comes from the friction between them.**


It's a great example of anthropomorphizing what a brand already sells.


**Design lesson:** An ensemble of characters creates far more narrative possibilities than a single mascot could.


### 7. The Pillsbury Doughboy (Pillsbury)


The Pillsbury Doughboy (Poppin' Fresh) was designed to feel soft, warm and playful. Since his 1965 debut, one of his defining traits has been his giggle when someone pokes his belly.


**That interaction became part of the character's identity.** It shows that memorable mascot design isn't only about appearance. Sound, movement and behavior can become just as recognizable.


**Design lesson:** Design your mascot's sound, movement and behavior from the start.


### 8. Chester Cheetah (Cheetos)


When Cheetos introduced Chester Cheetah in 1986, his sunglasses, relaxed posture and swagger gave a simple corn snack its own attitude.


Chester later faced pressure as scrutiny of food marketing to children increased. **But the character endured, which shows the value of a mascot with a clear, distinctive personality.**


**Design lesson:** Let the character express the personality you want people to associate with your brand.


### 9. The Energizer Bunny (Energizer)


The Energizer Bunny brings the brand's promise to life through movement. Since 1989, his defining trait has been simple: He just keeps going.


**That makes motion central to the character.** In a static image, you see a toy bunny. In motion, you understand what he stands for: energy, endurance and momentum.


**Design lesson:** If movement expresses your brand promise, build it into the mascot from the get-go.


### 10. Duo (Duolingo)


Duolingo's owl, Duo, arrived with the app in 2011 as a friendly interface character, more a functional piece of product design than a traditional mascot. Then the brand gave him a hilarious personality, and the character quickly outgrew the app.


What Duolingo did may feel uncomfortable for many teams: It developed the owl's personality well after launch. **The team knew, however, that consistency would be essential.** The same slightly unhinged voice had to show up again and again across its marketing so audiences would recognize Duo as a character, not a one-off joke.


**Design lesson:** Personality is an asset you can build after launch. The mascot just needs clear rules.


### 11. Scrub Daddy (Scrub Daddy)


Scrub Daddy is one of the rare cases where the mascot and the product are the same object.


Since the brand launched in 2012, its cheerful face has been molded into the sponge you buy. **That makes the character inseparable from the purchase.**


Scrub Daddy also combines mascot, product and packaging design, which is why it works so well on social: Every piece of content is a character post and a product demo at the same time.


**Design lesson:** The strongest possible product mascot is one your customer can physically hold.


### 12. Kevin the Carrot (Aldi UK)


Aldi UK introduced Kevin the Carrot in 2016 as the star of its Christmas campaigns. Each year, the character returns in a new story filled with adventure and romance, helping Aldi sell its festive range.


**Kevin's design is deliberately simple: He's essentially a carrot with eyes.** That keeps the focus on the stories Aldi tells around him each year, while repetition and consistency strengthen recognition over time.


**Design lesson:** Commit to a returning character with a strong story, and let repetition do the heavy lifting.

And if you want to meet the people behind some of the world's best-known marks, start with our list of the[most famous graphic designers](https://www.superside.com/blog/most-famous-graphic-designers) .


## Mascot, brand character or logo: The important distinctions


These three terms are often used interchangeably, which causes real confusion in briefs. Here's how they differ:


- **A brand logo:** A fixed, identifying mark that stays constant as part of a brand's identity. The Nike swoosh is a great example.
- **A brand character:** Any recurring character device a brand owns. Although it recurs, it may not be embodied. It could be a recognizable figure, voice or personality that appears again and again in the brand's marketing.
- **A mascot:** A distinctive, embodied character that acts as the brand's face. It makes the brand more recognizable and relatable, and it's meant to leave a lasting impression.


**Every mascot is a brand character, but not every brand character is a mascot.** A few famous brand mascots, like KFC's Colonel, genuinely work as both a mascot and a logo.


Getting this right in the brief helps you avoid a common mistake: commissioning a mascot when the strategy really calls for a simpler[corporate logo](https://www.superside.com/blog/corporate-logo-design) or a[visual identity](https://www.superside.com/blog/creating-a-visual-identity) refresh.


## The evidence: Why characters pay off


**Distinctive brand characters can outperform more conventional brand assets.**


Ipsos and Jones Knowles Ritchie tested 5,000+ brand assets with 26,000+ consumers worldwide and found that only 15% were truly distinctive.


Assets rated "gold" were the ones most strongly and uniquely linked to the right brand.[Marketing Week reported](https://www.marketingweek.com/15-brand-assets-truly-distinctive-finds-research/) that 16% of brand characters achieved gold status, compared with only 6% of slogans and 4% of brand colors.


Their impact on business performance is also well documented.[Research by System1 using IPA data](https://lbbonline.com/news/research-by-system1-shows-memorable-characters-in-ads-boost-chances-of-profit-by-30) found that campaigns built around fluent devices (recurring characters or scenarios) were:


- **37%** more likely to grow market share
- **27%** more likely to increase customer gains
- **30%** more likely to grow profit


The same research found that in the US, brands using memorable characters as fluent devices are almost 50% more likely to earn three Stars or higher on System1's ad ratings and three times more likely to hit five Stars, a score System1 links to market share growth.


Fluent-device use in IPA Effectiveness Awards entries fell from 41% in 1992 to just 12%, which means the industry walked away from one of its most reliable tools. Orlando Wood, Chief Innovation Officer at System1, put the value plainly in the same research, noting that "fluent devices help advertisers build long-term memory structures."


Marketing effectiveness consultant Peter Field has tracked the wider decline.[In his IPA report The Crisis in Creative Effectiveness](https://ipa.co.uk/knowledge/publications-reports/the-crisis-in-creative-effectiveness) , he argued that short-termism has driven a collapse in the effectiveness and efficiency of creative work.


The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute's Professor Jenni Romaniuk sets a clear bar for any[distinctive brand asset](https://marketingscience.info/news-and-insights/brands-of-distinction) : It must be unique (it only evokes your brand) and famous (everyone who sees it thinks of your brand), and uniqueness matters most. A well-built character can score high on both.


### The recent proof that mascots are brand gold


System1's[November 2025 analysis of festive advertising](https://system1group.com/blog/its-never-too-late-to-build-a-brand-character) found that four of the top 10 ads in its early read of the season featured brand-owned characters:


- **Aldi's Kevin the Carrot:** Achieved the highest 10-second Star Rating ever recorded in System1's database.
- **Very's Pink Flamingos:** Drove retail sales up 2.3% year on year against a market growing just 0.5%, with cost efficiency for driving recall up 15% by year two.
- **Boots' Puss in Boots:** Debuted with a 5.2 Star Rating for long-term potential.


**One caveat matters for budgeting.** The same analysis says you need to keep going for around three years before a character starts to deliver its real benefits. A mascot is a long-term investment, not a one-campaign stunt.


### The licensing opportunity you need to know


Once a character earns recognition, licensing can extend its commercial value.


Global retail sales of licensed merchandise and services reached $389.8 billion in 2025, up 5.45% year over year, according to[Licensing International's 2026 Global Licensing Industry Study](https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/licensing-international-2026-global-study-190000452.html) . **Character and entertainment was the largest category, with $161.8 billion in retail sales, up 8%.**


## How a mascot can become a reusable asset


Designing a mascot is relatively easy. **The real challenge is keeping that character consistent across hundreds of touchpoints and formats.**


The table below sums up what typically goes wrong and how to avoid it:


What goes wrong Why it happens How to prevent it


The character's expression is inconsistent Multiple hands, no shared rules Create and use a character bible with hard rules


The mascot fails on small assets Designed only at large, hero scale Write specs that cover both extremes


The character can't react Only one pose was ever drawn Develop a defined expression range


Motion feels off-brand Personality never translated to movement Set movement and timing rules from the start


Volume kills quality Manual production under tight deadlines A shared brand system applied to every asset


### Design for reuse from the first sketch


A mascot that only works in one pose and at one angle is a thousand missed opportunities. **Build scalable characters as systems from day one.** Think[smart illustration design](https://www.superside.com/illustration-design-services) that includes:


- A full set of reference views, so the character stays consistent from every angle
- An expression range, so it can react rather than just stand there
- Locked proportions and color values
- Behavioral rules that define what the character does and doesn't do
- Format-specific guidance for small, large and animated applications


This is where[illustration design](https://www.superside.com/blog/what-is-illustration-design) stops being about one beautiful image and becomes about a repeatable asset.


### Write the character bible


**The most valuable document in any mascot program is the one that says what the character can't do.** Recognition depends on constraints. Without them, a mascot drawn by five different people becomes five different mascots.


With a character bible, a small or distributed team can produce hundreds of on-brand assets that still read as one character. It's standard[brand identity practice](https://www.superside.com/blog/brand-identity) applied to a mascot, and it belongs inside the same system as the rest of[your branding guide](https://www.superside.com/blog/branding-guide) .


### Hold the line across formats


Your character has to work in a vertical Instagram Story, a square feed post, a wide banner and a YouTube Short.


Many brand characters break at the extremes, in tiny app icons and oversized billboards, so your spec sheet should cover both ends.


**That's exactly the job a strong[corporate visual identity](https://www.superside.com/blog/corporate-visual-identity-design) system is built to do.**


### Understand what can go wrong


The most common failure is drift: a slightly different smile here, an off color there, until the character no longer matches its own origin.


**Drift is rarely a talent problem.** It creeps in when there's no shared brand system and knowledge lives only in people's heads. A brand system that carries your rules into every brief closes that gap.


**That's what[Brand Brain](https://www.superside.com/brandbrain) , Superside's AI context engine, is built to do.**


### Be honest about AI


AI can help you build out and extend your brand character. It can generate asset variations, adapt a locked character across formats at speed and take repetitive volume off your creative team.


**However, AI can't invent an original, standout character.** The concept, personality and single confident decision at the heart of every enduring mascot come from human creative judgment.


Our guides to[experimenting with illustration](https://www.superside.com/blog/experiment-with-illustration) and[AI prompts for logo design](https://www.superside.com/blog/ai-prompts-logo-design) treat AI the way it works best: as an amplifier of a human idea.


## Bringing a mascot to life in motion


Today's mascots need to work in video and social content, so[motion design](https://www.superside.com/blog/motion-graphic-examples) should be part of the character from the start. **Motion is where personality becomes unmistakable** , and it makes the brand more recognizable.


That means the character bible should include clear movement rules. **How does it walk, react, celebrate or sulk?**


A change in pace, gesture or expression can make the same character feel completely different, so it's best to refine these movements early. For inspiration, our roundup of[corporate animation examples](https://www.superside.com/blog/corporate-animation-examples) shows how brands translate personality into movement.


Achieving scale is typically the toughest part. If a mascot appears in several short-form videos and multiple ad versions every week, you need a production team and[design system](https://www.superside.com/design-systems) that can keep up.


AI systems can help increase output, but only if the core character stays fixed. **The teams behind the best brand mascots know AI needs tight rules and strong human oversight.**

The famous brand mascots in this article share two things: a clear creative idea and a system that protected it over time.


**That system matters more as people, formats and channels multiply.** Clear rules for proportion, color, expression, motion and use keep the character recognizable without limiting creative flexibility, and that's what turns a drawing into an asset that keeps performing year after year.

## FAQs


A good mascot is built on one strong creative decision and an ongoing commitment to it. It should be unique and famous, rooted in something true about the product and backed by a clear personality and rules for consistent use.


Costs vary widely. A simple static character costs less than a full mascot system with multiple poses and expressions, usage guidelines, animation and ongoing content production. Price depends mainly on the number of assets and formats, the level of animation and the scope of the character system.


A[logo](https://www.superside.com/blog/logo-design-inspiration-examples) is a fixed visual identifier. A mascot is a character with a personality that can move, react and appear in different poses or scenarios. Put simply, a logo identifies and a mascot performs.


AI is great at extending a mascot: generating variations, adapting a locked character across formats and handling repetitive production at speed. It's weak at inventing the core idea. The concept and personality that make a character work still come from human creative judgment, so AI works best as an amplifier for a human-designed character.


Old mascots give brands something valuable: instant recognition. A familiar character revives brand memory the company already paid to build, adds personality to digital content and gives new campaigns a distinctive asset in feeds full of look-alike visuals.


Start with a clear character system that defines the mascot's look, personality and movement. Then create reusable motion rules for expressions, gestures and actions so the character stays consistent across posts, videos and ad formats. AI systems can help your team produce more content, but only when they work from clear brand rules.
